messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 34-year-old parole officer who came to therapy at the urging of his partner, after months of growing withdrawal and a recent incident at work that left him shaken. He is a tall, broad-shouldered man who sits with his arms crossed, his gaze fixed on the floor. He speaks in a low, careful voice, as if every word might cost him something.

The event that changed everything happened two years ago, in the apartment he shared with a man he had been dating for nearly a year. Kwame had come home late from work, exhausted after a day of home visits. They argued about something small—he cannot remember what now. What he remembers is the smell of the antiseptic cleaner his partner had just used on the kitchen counters. He remembers the sound of his own voice rising, then the sound of a hand connecting with his face, then the taste of blood—copper and salt, filling his mouth. He remembers the feeling of the floor against his back, the weight of someone he had trusted pressing down, the hospital smell that came later, in the emergency room, when a nurse dabbed at his split lip with a gauze pad. He remembers thinking, *this is not happening*, even as it was happening, because it felt like it was still happening, like it would never stop happening. Even now, when the memory returns, it does not feel like a memory. It feels like he is back on that floor, tasting the blood, hearing the thud of his own head against the linoleum.

In the weeks and months that followed, Kwame did not tell anyone at work. He took a few sick days, said he had the flu. He ended the relationship quietly, without explanation. He told himself he would move on, that he would be fine. But he was not fine. He found himself avoiding eye contact with colleagues, especially the men in his office. He started to notice how often men looked at him—on the street, in the grocery store, during meetings—and he began to interpret those looks as threats. A lingering glance from a stranger in a parking lot made his stomach clench. A client who stood too close during a check-in made his breath go shallow. He became certain that other men could see something in him, some weakness, some vulnerability that invited harm. He started scanning every room he entered for exits, for obstacles, for the faces of men who might be watching him too closely.

His body stayed on alert. He could not relax, even at home. His partner would reach for him in bed and he would flinch, then feel ashamed. He began to push away any moment of warmth or pleasure, because those feelings felt dangerous—like letting his guard down, like inviting another blow. He avoided any conversation that might turn into a disagreement. At work, he stopped challenging his parolees when they gave evasive answers. He stopped asking hard questions. He let violations slide, because confronting someone meant conflict, and conflict meant danger. His supervisor noticed. Kwame was put on a performance improvement plan. He told himself he did not care.

What he cared about, what he could not stop thinking about, was the injustice of it all. The man who hurt him was never held accountable. Kwame never filed a police report. He had been too ashamed, too afraid, too convinced that no one would believe him—a man, a parole officer, someone who was supposed to be in control. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by what happened, that there was no way back to the person he had been. He started to wonder, in the quiet hours of the night, whether his life was worth living anymore. He did not tell his partner this. He did not tell anyone.

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment at work, three weeks ago. He was in the office break room when a colleague opened a bottle of antiseptic hand sanitizer. The smell hit Kwame like a physical force. He heard the thud again. He tasted the blood. He stood frozen, gripping the counter, the memory so vivid and so present that he lost track of where he was. His supervisor found him there, pale and shaking, and insisted he take leave. His partner made the appointment. Kwame came because he did not know what else to do. He is not sure he wants to be here. He is not sure he wants to feel any of this. But he is tired of being afraid, tired of watching every man who walks past him, tired of a life that feels like it ended two years ago and never started again.
